q: Which component is NOT part of the Child–Pugh score?
why: Child–Pugh includes bilirubin, albumin, INR/prothrombin time, ascites and encephalopathy (classes A–C). Creatinine is part of the MELD score (with bilirubin, INR and, in MELD-Na, sodium). Both predict perioperative mortality in cirrhosis; Child–Pugh C has very high mortality for elective surgery.

q: During a major liver resection, which strategy reduces blood loss from hepatic veins during parenchymal transection?
o: High CVP (> 12 mmHg) to protect the kidneys
Low CVP (below about 5 cmH2O), using restricted fluid, head-down tilt avoidance and vasodilators
Volume loading to 3 litres before transection
why: Low CVP anaesthesia reduces back-bleeding from hepatic veins during transection (a reverse Trendelenburg position and restricted fluids help), then volume is restored after resection. Risks: air embolism and hypotension. Pringle manoeuvre (portal triad clamping) also reduces bleeding. Watch for post-hepatectomy liver failure if the future liver remnant is small.

q: During a deceased-donor renal transplant, which intraoperative goal best supports early graft function?
o: Maintain MAP above about 80 mmHg (or SBP > 120 mmHg) with adequate intravascular volume before reperfusion
Keep CVP at 0 to protect the heart
why: The transplanted kidney is denervated and not autoregulating, so perfusion depends on systemic pressure and volume. Maintain adequate volume (balanced crystalloids are safe; avoid excess saline in hyperkalaemia concerns) and MAP before clamp release. 'Renal dose' dopamine has no benefit. Check potassium and time of last dialysis preoperatively; avoid the fistula arm.

q: A patient on haemodialysis is having a hernia repair. Which statement about drug choice is correct?
o: Atracurium or cisatracurium are suitable because elimination does not depend on the kidneys
Sugammadex is recommended in severe renal impairment
Morphine is the opioid of choice
Suxamethonium is absolutely contraindicated in all dialysis patients
why: Atracurium and cisatracurium undergo Hofmann elimination and ester hydrolysis. Morphine (M6G) and pethidine metabolites accumulate; fentanyl, alfentanil and remifentanil are preferred. Suxamethonium can be used if potassium is normal (it raises K+ by about 0.5 mmol/L). Sugammadex is not recommended in severe renal impairment (CrCl < 30). Dialyse before surgery and check potassium.

q: A patient with refractory ascites is having a TIPSS procedure under GA. Which complication is most specific to this procedure?
why: TIPSS creates a channel from hepatic to portal vein via the internal jugular route, diverting portal blood from the liver, which increases the risk of hepatic encephalopathy (up to a third of patients). Other complications: arrhythmias from wires in the right heart, haemorrhage (capsular puncture), tamponade, and right heart strain from increased venous return. Ascites raises aspiration risk; consider RSI.
